f-date.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-oracle-second.claim: The envoys returned as suppliants carrying olive branches and were given a second answer: Zeus grants that a wooden wall alone shall not be taken.

f-oracle-hedge.claim: Some older Athenians believed the wooden wall meant the thorn hedge that once ringed the Acropolis.

f-evacuation.claim: The Athenians evacuated their families and slaves to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis.

f-defenders.claim: A few Athenians, the temple stewards and poor men, stayed on the Acropolis behind a barricade of planks and timber, believing it was the wooden wall of the oracle.

f-climb.claim: The Persians climbed the steep front of the Acropolis near the shrine of Aglauros, where no guard was posted.

f-burned.claim: They killed the defenders, plundered the temple and set the whole Acropolis on fire.

f-susa.claim: Xerxes sent a horseman to Susa to announce his success.

f-olive.claim: Herodotus says Athena's sacred olive tree burned with the temple, yet the next day a new shoot a cubit long had grown from the stump.

f-panic.claim: When news reached the Greek fleet at Salamis that the Acropolis had fallen, some commanders panicked and voted to sail away to the Isthmus.

f-athens-ships.claim: Athens supplied the largest contingent of the Greek fleet: 180 ships.
